question.brief: Ania, 27, earns 5,800 PLN a month after tax, plus 0 to 1,500 PLN from freelance work that she only knows about when the month starts. She needs 4,800 PLN for essentials. She has a 4,000 PLN buffer and 3,000 PLN of card debt at 20% a year; the card takes a 3% minimum payment every month. Two bills come once a year: car insurance, 1,800 PLN, in month 9, and a holiday, 2,500 PLN, in month 14. She can keep money in her buffer or a bills pot, or invest it in a broad share fund, an inflation-indexed savings bond (1% fee if sold early) or shares of one company, CrocoTech. Write her monthly rule for 24 months. Two tests must pass: a 2-month job loss, whenever it comes, never makes her borrow on the card, and she invests at least 12,000 PLN. Then we test your rule against other surprises.

assumptions: Freelance income is drawn at random for each month between 0 and 1,500 PLN; in a job-loss month there is no income at all.
The buffer pays 4% a year. Card debt costs 20% a year; the minimum payment, 3% of the debt, is taken first each month.
A yearly bill is paid from the bills pot first, then from the month's money, then the buffer, then the card.

Returns come from our fictional market. The bond pays about 0.35% a month (inflation plus a margin, illustrative) and costs 1% if sold early. CrocoTech has about the same average as the fund, but a much wider spread and rare large falls.

The surprises and their likelihoods are illustrative, chosen for teaching.
After the tests, your rule also runs through 200 random 10-year futures: how often it never borrowed on the card, and how much it grew (median), compared with the reference solution = 100.

reveal.editorial: The reference rule works in order. Until the buffer covers 2 months, all spare money goes there, because a job loss can come early. After that, it puts aside each month the part of the next yearly bill that is still missing, so a bill never eats the buffer. Then it pays off the card, because 20% a year beats any expected return. Then it fills the buffer to 3 months, and only then invests: most in the broad fund, the rest in the indexed bond. The bond's early-sale fee is why the buffer is not kept there. CrocoTech has about the same average return as the fund but a far wider spread, so its typical result is lower: one company is not a diversified investment.

question.brief: Marek, 35, has 100,000 PLN invested: 60% in a broad share fund and 40% in a bond fund. He adds 1,000 PLN every month. His goal, his daughter's studies, is 10 years away, so his target share of shares falls from 60% to 40% over those years. Every trade costs 0.29%, at least 5 PLN, and 19% tax is due each year on the gains he realises by selling. Write his rule for the 10 years. Two tests must pass: in a long rally his shares stay within 10 points of the month's target, and in a crash, whenever it comes, they never fall more than 20 points below it, so no panic selling. Then we test your rule in other markets.

assumptions: Fund returns come from our fictional market: calm and stress periods, with bonds falling a little when shares fall hard. Not a forecast; real history replaces it once the data is loaded.
Marek's target share of shares falls in a straight line from 60% in month 1 to 40% in month 120.
Every buy or sell costs 0.29% of the money traded, at least 5 PLN. Rebalancing is one sale and one purchase.

Tax: 19% of the year's net realised gains, paid every 12th month; losses are not carried into the next year. Gains are measured against the average price paid, a simplification of the real rules (which match a sale to the oldest purchase first). No IKE or IKZE.
Marek has a 6-month buffer, so the tests are about his investments, not his budget.
The market scenarios and their likelihoods are illustrative, chosen for teaching.
After the tests, your rule also runs through 200 random 10-year futures: growth compared with the reference solution = 100.
obligatory: A long rally: shares +1.5% a month for 10 years; stay within 10 points of the target
A crash, whenever it comes: shares -15% two months in a row; never more than 20 points below the target

reveal.editorial: The reference rule does two things. It puts each month's new money into whichever fund is below its target, which steers the mix back for the price of one small trade and without selling, so no tax. It rebalances only when the mix is more than 5 points off and the money to move is worth more than 1,000 PLN, so the minimum fee does not eat small trades. Because the target falls every month, a rule that keeps 60/40 drifts away from what Marek needs as his goal comes closer. Rebalancing every month keeps the mix tight but pays fees and tax again and again. In a crash, the rule buys shares when they are cheap, which is the opposite of panic selling.
